cited_details.statement: Person search aims to localize and identify a target individual across a large gallery of uncropped scene images, integrating pedestrian detection and re-identification into a single retrieval problem, and is particularly valuable for public-safety surveillance and social-governance applications [https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.01850].

introduced an end-to-end Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) that jointly handles detection and re-identification, avoiding error propagation from a conventional two-stage pipeline [http://www.ee.cuhk.edu.hk/~xgwang/PS/dataset.html].

To support this research, the authors released the CUHK-SYSU benchmark, comprising 18,184 images and 8,432 identities harvested from street photographs and movie stills [https://hyper.ai/en/datasets/17981].

A central technical contribution of that work is the Online Instance Matching (OIM) loss, which addresses long-tailed identity distributions by maintaining a labeled feature queue together with an unlabeled feature table for comparison [https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.01850].

By avoiding the need for exhaustive pairwise similarity computations, OIM scales gracefully to gallery sizes that would be infeasible for traditional metric-learning losses [https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.01850].

The OIM loss has become a canonical supervision signal for person search, providing a scalable alternative to standard softmax under sparse and unbalanced identity labels [https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.01850].

further showed that sequential training of the detector and re-identification sub-networks remains competitive with fully joint optimization, indicating that the two tasks can be effectively decoupled when training data is sufficient [https://cea.hal.science/cea-03251768/document].

formalized the task with a deep reinforcement-learning agent that recursively crops candidate regions in gallery images, learning a policy that aligns each candidate crop with the textual query [https://arxiv.org/abs/1809.00365].
This early work demonstrated that text queries can guide region proposal and ranking without relying on bounding-box supervision at inference time [https://arxiv.org/abs/1809.00365].

proposed the Deep Adversarial Graph Attention Convolution Network (A-GANet), which constructs visual and textual scene graphs encoding object attributes and pairwise relationships, then aligns the two modalities through adversarial training [https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/56e3758cd9acc97f41ed3dbefd66fd76f238e4fb].

developed a generative adversarial framework that learns modality-invariant embeddings for text-to-image matching, directly applicable to text-based person search by forcing image and text encoders into a shared latent space [https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.10534].

In image-based re-identification, multi-level fusion of global and local features improves robustness to pose, occlusion, and viewpoint changes by combining holistic identity cues with body-part details [https://www.mdpi.com/1999-4893/13/5/111].

Such architectures typically combine a global branch encoding whole-body appearance with part-based branches focused on head, torso, and limbs, capturing complementary cues at multiple spatial granularities [https://www.mdpi.com/1999-4893/13/5/111].

For text-based retrieval, scene-graph representations encode fine-grained attribute relations that bag-of-words embeddings cannot capture, yielding richer visual-textual correspondences for matching pedestrian images to descriptive sentences [https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/56e3758cd9acc97f41ed3dbefd66fd76f238e4fb].

By treating each image and sentence as a graph of attribute and relationship nodes, the model can align entities rather than relying solely on holistic global embeddings [https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/56e3758cd9acc97f41ed3dbefd66fd76f238e4fb].

The OIM loss implements a scalable online comparison against a labeled queue and an unlabeled memory bank, avoiding the prohibitive cost of exhaustive pairwise comparisons over large galleries [https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.01850].

Triplet-based objectives explicitly pull same-identity pairs together while pushing different-identity pairs apart in the embedding space, and online instance-matching variants have been shown to mine shared-identity cues across non-overlapping camera views [https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.10560].

In the text-based setting, adversarial alignment closes the modality gap by forcing image and text encoders into a shared embedding space, an approach validated across multiple retrieval benchmarks [https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.10534].

mitigates this by sharing backbone features between the detection and re-identification heads, allowing OIM gradients to regularize the detection pathway and enforce identity-driven detection [https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.01850].

The shared backbone pattern also reduces computational redundancy at inference, since a single forward pass produces both the detection output and the re-identification embedding for every proposal [https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.01850].

This identity-driven detection pattern is reiterated in later work, where the re-id branch is co-trained with the detector to enforce consistency between the two objectives throughout the network [https://cea.hal.science/cea-03251768/document].

Complementary research reformulated re-identification as regressing a continuous identity vector rather than classifying discrete identities, offering an alternative mechanism to align detection and identification features and to scale gracefully to large open-world populations [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6411216/].

evidence.title: Deep Adversarial Graph Attention Convolution Network for Text-Based Person Search
evidence.abstract: The newly emerging text-based person search task aims at retrieving the target pedestrian by a query in natural language with fine-grained description of a pedestrian. It is more applicable in reality without the requirement of image/video query of a pedestrian, as compared to image/video based person search, i.e., person re-identification. In this work, we propose a novel deep adversarial graph attention convolution network (A-GANet) for text-based person search. The A-GANet exploits both textual and visual scene graphs, consisting of object properties and relationships, from the text queries and gallery images of pedestrians, towards learning informative textual and visual representations. It learns an effective joint textual-visual latent feature space in adversarial learning manner, bridging modality gap and facilitating pedestrian matching. Specifically, the A-GANet consists of an image graph attention network, a text graph attention network and an adversarial learning module. The image and text graph attention networks are designed with a novel graph attention convolution layer, which effectively exploits graph structure in the learning of textual and visual features, leading to precise and discriminative representations. An adversarial learning module is developed with a feature transformer and a modality discriminator, to learn a joint textual-visual feature space for cross-modality matching. Extensive experimental results on two challenging benchmarks, i.e., CUHK-PEDES and Flickr30k datasets, have demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed method.

evidence.title: Adversarial Representation Learning for Text-to-Image Matching
evidence.abstract: For many computer vision applications such as image captioning, visual question answering, and person search, learning discriminative feature representations at both image and text level is an essential yet challenging problem. Its challenges originate from the large word variance in the text domain as well as the difficulty of accurately measuring the distance between the features of the two modalities. Most prior work focuses on the latter challenge, by introducing loss functions that help the network learn better feature representations but fail to account for the complexity of the textual input. With that in mind, we introduce TIMAM: a Text-Image Modality Adversarial Matching approach that learns modality-invariant feature representations using adversarial and cross-modal matching objectives. In addition, we demonstrate that BERT, a publicly-available language model that extracts word embeddings, can successfully be applied in the text-to-image matching domain. The proposed approach achieves state-of-the-art cross-modal matching performance on four widely-used publicly-available datasets resulting in absolute improvements ranging from 2% to 5% in terms of rank-1 accuracy.

evidence.title: Learning Semantic-Aligned Feature Representation for Text-Based Person Search
evidence.abstract: Text-based person search aims to retrieve images of a certain pedestrian by a textual description. The key challenge of this task is to eliminate the inter-modality gap and achieve the feature alignment across modalities. In this paper, we propose a semantic-aligned embedding method for text-based person search, in which the feature alignment across modalities is achieved by automatically learning the semantic-aligned visual features and textual features. First, we introduce two Transformer-based backbones to encode robust feature representations of the images and texts. Second, we design a semantic-aligned feature aggregation network to adaptively select and aggregate features with the same semantics into part-aware features, which is achieved by a multi-head attention module constrained by a cross-modality part alignment loss and a diversity loss. Experimental results on the CUHK-PEDES and Flickr30K datasets show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performances.

evidence.title: A survey of transfer learning
evidence.abstract: Machine learning and data mining techniques have been used in numerous real-world applications. An assumption of traditional machine learning methodologies is the training data and testing data are taken from the same domain, such that the input feature space and data distribution characteristics are the same. However, in some real-world machine learning scenarios, this assumption does not hold. There are cases where training data is expensive or difficult to collect. Therefore, there is a need to create high-performance learners trained with more easily obtained data from different domains. This methodology is referred to as transfer learning. This survey paper formally defines transfer learning, presents information on current solutions, and reviews applications applied to transfer learning. Lastly, there is information listed on software downloads for various transfer learning solutions and a discussion of possible future research work. The transfer learning solutions surveyed are independent of data size and can be applied to big data environments.
